events.title: Groovy 1.0 released
events.summary: The Groovy team shipped Groovy 1.0 on January 5, 2007 — a dynamic [JVM] language with [Ruby]/[Python]-style syntax and [Java] interoperability.
events.about: Groovy scripts [Gradle] build files, Jenkins pipelines, and Grails web apps — you call [Java] libraries directly while writing less boilerplate. Closures, builders, and optional typing made it popular for testing (Spock) and DSLs before [Kotlin] rose on [Android].

narrative.whyChosen: Groovy 1.0 was the first stable dynamic language designed to run on the [JVM] beside [Java].
narrative.whyImportant: It proved [JVM] [bytecode] could host scripting languages and later powered [Gradle], the default [Android]/[Java] build tool.
narrative.problemSolved: [Java] was verbose for scripting and DSLs; developers wanted [Ruby]-like ergonomics without leaving the [Java] ecosystem.

events.title: Steve Jobs introduces the iPhone
events.summary: Steve Jobs unveiled the [iPhone] at Macworld on January 9, 2007 — combining a phone, iPod, and internet communicator.
events.about: The [iPhone] shifted mobile computing from feature phones and BlackBerry keyboards to touch-first smartphones — spawning the [App Store] economy and mobile-first web development.

narrative.whyChosen: The [iPhone] redefined personal computing around mobile apps and touch [UI].
narrative.whyImportant: It made mobile web and native apps central to how software is built and consumed.
narrative.problemSolved: Phones were clumsy for browsing and lacked a unified pocket computer experience.

events.title: Reed Hastings launches Netflix streaming
events.summary: Netflix launched its Watch Now streaming service on January 16, 2007 — pivoting from [DVD]-by-mail to internet video.
events.about: Hastings and Marc Randolph built Netflix into the default streaming platform — changing how developers build CDNs, encode video, and serve global audiences. The shift from discs to bytes redefined entertainment technology.

narrative.whyChosen: Netflix streaming launched the mainstream era of over-the-top video.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved internet delivery could replace physical media for mass-market entertainment.
narrative.problemSolved: Consumers waited days for DVDs when broadband could deliver video on demand.
